# From Estimation to Testing {.section-slide}

From a range of plausible values to a yes/no question.

## A different kind of question

::: {.box}
A confidence interval gives a **range of plausible values** for a parameter. Research often asks something sharper: *is the parameter equal to a particular value?*
:::

. . .

::: {.box .key}
<span class="tag">Definition</span>
**Hypothesis testing** is a decision-making framework used to evaluate specific claims about a population.
:::

## Examples from the class survey

| Topic | Estimation | Hypothesis testing |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Heights** | What is the average height of students in this class? | Is it equal to $167$ cm? |
| **Demography** | What is the average number of children per family in Kazakhstan? | Is it greater than $2.1$, the replacement rate? |
| **Emigration** | What share of students is willing to emigrate from Kazakhstan? | Are girls more willing to emigrate than boys? |
| **Study hours** | How many hours do students study for this class on average? | Do girls study more than boys? |
| **Difficulty** | By how much does one more unit of perceived difficulty change study hours? | Does difficulty affect study hours at all? |

## Estimation vs. testing

::: {.cards}
::: {.box .c}
<span class="tag">Estimation asks</span>
What is a good guess for $\mu$?
:::
::: {.box .key .c}
<span class="tag">Testing asks</span>
Is the data consistent with a specific value $\mu_0$?
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.box .good}
<span class="tag">Hint</span>
Every test question has a **benchmark**: $167$ cm, $2.1$ children, girls and boys equally willing, equal study hours, no effect. This benchmark is the **null hypothesis** $H_0$.
:::

# The two-sided test: the recipe {.section-slide}

Four steps, one example: testing $\mu$ when $\sigma$ is known.

## Our example

::: {.box .key}
<span class="tag">Question</span>
Is the average height of students taking this class equal to $167$ cm?
:::

. . .

::: {.box}
<span class="tag">We have asked this before</span>
In the estimation lecture, to decide whether a value was a **reasonable guess** for $\mu$, we asked: *if this value were true, how surprising would our sample be?* Very surprising: not a reasonable guess. Not surprising: a reasonable guess.
:::

. . .

::: {.box .good}
<span class="tag">The bridge</span>
That is exactly what hypothesis testing does, for **one specific guess**: here, $\mu=167$. The confidence interval ran this check for every possible guess at once. Now we make each step precise, and give it a name.
:::

## Our example: the data

::: {.box}
Data: $n=20$, $\bar{X}=170$ cm, and $\sigma=8$ cm is assumed **known**: the same student-heights example as in the estimation lecture. There we found the 95% interval $[166.49,\ 173.51]$.
:::

. . .

::: {.box .key}
Our task: measure how surprising $\bar{X}=170$ (or something even further from $167$) is **if** the true mean were $167$.
:::

. . .

::: {.cards}
::: {.box .warn .c}
<span class="tag">Very surprising</span>
There is **statistical evidence against** the claim that the true mean is $167$.
:::
::: {.box .good .c}
<span class="tag">Not very surprising</span>
There is **not enough evidence against** the claim that the true mean is $167$.
:::
:::

## Step 1: Formulate hypotheses

::: {.cards}
::: {.box .c}
<span class="tag">Null hypothesis $H_0$</span>
The status quo, the "boring" result: no effect, no difference. The benchmark we try to **find evidence against**.
:::
::: {.box .key .c}
<span class="tag">Alternative $H_1$</span>
The research claim, the "interesting" result: there **is** an effect or a difference.
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.box}
If we find enough evidence to **reject** $H_0$, we favour $H_1$.
:::

## Hypotheses: the rules

::: {.cards}
::: {.box}
<span class="tag">$H_0$</span>
**Must always contain an equality sign**: $=$, $\leq$ or $\geq$.
:::
::: {.box .key}
<span class="tag">$H_1$</span>
**Never contains an equality sign**: $\mathrel{\rlap{\,/}{=}}$, $>$ or $<$.
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.box .good}
<span class="tag">Example: two-sided test</span>
$$H_0:\ \mu=167 \qquad H_1:\ \mu\mathrel{\rlap{\,/}{=}}167$$
:::

## Step 2: The test statistic

::: {.box}
The test statistic measures the **distance** between the sample result and the null, in standard errors. With $\sigma$ known we use the $z$-statistic:
$$z=\frac{\bar{X}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}$$
:::

. . .

::: {.box .key}
<span class="tag">Definition</span>
$z$ counts how many standard errors the observed $\bar{X}$ is from the hypothesized $\mu_0$. Under $H_0$, by the CLT, $z$ is **approximately** $N(0,1)$ (exactly, if the population is normal).
:::

## Test statistic: our data

::: {.box .key}
$$z=\frac{170-167}{8/\sqrt{20}}=\frac{3}{1.789}\approx1.68$$
:::

. . .

::: {.box}
Our sample mean is about **1.7 standard errors above** the benchmark. Is that far enough to doubt $H_0$?
:::

## Step 3: The p-value

::: {.box}
**Assume $H_0$ is true.** Then the distribution of $\bar{X}$ (and of $z$) is fully known. We can ask how likely it is to get a sample **at least as extreme** as ours.
:::

. . .

::: {.box .key}
<span class="tag">Definition</span>
The **p-value** is the probability, computed assuming $H_0$ is true, that the test statistic takes a value as extreme as, or more extreme than (relative to $H_0$), the one actually observed.
:::

. . .

::: {.cards}
::: {.box .warn .c}
<span class="tag">Small p-value</span>
"If $H_0$ were true, this sample would be a near-impossible miracle."
:::
::: {.box .good .c}
<span class="tag">Large p-value</span>
"This sample is exactly what we would expect under $H_0$."
:::
:::

## The p-value: our data

::: {.box .key}
$$p=2\,\Phi(-1.68)\approx0.093$$
:::

. . .

::: {.box}
If the true mean height were $167$ cm, we would get a sample mean at least as far from $167$ as $170$ (in either direction) only about **9%** of the time. This is the probability we saw in the estimation lecture for the candidate $\mu=167$.
:::

## Step 4: Choose $\alpha$ and decide

::: {.box}
The **significance level** $\alpha$ is a threshold, **chosen before looking at the data**: how much "surprise" we tolerate before we stop believing $H_0$. For $\alpha=0.05$: "I blame random chance for anything that happens more than 5% of the time."
:::

. . .

| Significance level $\alpha$ | Interpretation |
|:-:|:--|
| **0.10** | 10% risk of a false alarm. Moderate evidence required. |
| **0.05** | 5% risk of a false alarm. The standard benchmark. |
| **0.01** | 1% risk of a false alarm. Very strong evidence required. |

## The decision rule

| Condition | Intuition | Verdict |
|:-:|:--|:--|
| **$p<\alpha$** | Too rare to be a coincidence. | There is sufficient evidence: **reject $H_0$** in favour of $H_1$. |
| **$p\geq\alpha$** | Common enough to be random noise. | There is not sufficient evidence: **fail to reject $H_0$**. |

. . .

::: {.box .key}
<span class="tag">Evidence gauge</span>
The larger $|z|$, the smaller the p-value, and the more inconsistent the data is with $H_0$.
:::

## Decision: our data

::: {.box .good}
$p\approx0.093$. At $\alpha=0.05$ (and, of course, at $\alpha=0.01$) we **fail to reject** $H_0$: there is **not sufficient evidence** that the average height of students differs from $167$ cm.
:::

. . .

::: {.box .warn}
At the more lenient $\alpha=0.10$ we **would reject** $H_0$ ($0.093<0.10$): there **is sufficient evidence** at the 10% level that the average height differs from $167$ cm. The verdict depends on the threshold, so choose $\alpha$ first.
:::

. . .

::: {.box}
<span class="tag">Careful</span>
"Fail to reject" is **not** "$H_0$ is true". It only says the data is not surprising enough to rule it out.
:::

## What does $\alpha$ actually mean?

::: {.box .key}
<span class="tag">Definition</span>
$\alpha=P(\text{reject }H_0\mid H_0\text{ is true})$. With $\alpha=0.05$: if $H_0$ is true, about **5% of samples** will still make us reject it. This mistake is the **Type I error** (a false alarm).
:::

. . .

::: {.cards}
::: {.box .warn .c}
<span class="tag">Type I error</span>
Reject $H_0$ when it is **true**. Its probability is $\alpha$, which **we choose**.
:::
::: {.box .c}
<span class="tag">Type II error</span>
Fail to reject $H_0$ when it is **false**. We do not set it directly; **a larger $n$** makes it smaller.
:::
:::

## Critical values: the shortcut

::: {.box}
Instead of computing the p-value, compare $|z|$ with a **critical value** (from the table). It gives the **same verdict** as $p<\alpha$.
:::

. . .

| $\alpha$ | Two-sided: reject if $\lvert z\rvert>$ | One-sided: reject if $z>$ (or $z<-$) |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| **0.10** | $1.645$ | $1.282$ |
| **0.05** | $1.960$ | $1.645$ |
| **0.01** | $2.576$ | $2.326$ |

. . .

::: {.box .good}
<span class="tag">Our data</span>
$|z|=1.68<1.96$, so we **fail to reject** at $\alpha=0.05$ (same as $p=0.093>0.05$). But $1.68>1.645$, so we **reject** at $\alpha=0.10$ (same as before).
:::

## Confidence interval and test

::: {.cap}
A confidence interval and a **two-sided** test are two sides of the same coin. Move the hypothesized $\mu_0$ and watch the p-value and the intervals.
:::

<div class="readout" id="du-out"></div>

<div class="ctl" style="justify-content:center">
  <label>Hypothesized $\mu_0$: <input type="range" id="du-mu" min="161" max="179" step="0.01" value="167" style="width:420px"> <b id="du-mu-val">167.00</b></label>
</div>

<script>
(function () {
  var SE = 8 / Math.sqrt(20), XO = 170, L = 50, R = 880, XA = 155, XB = 181;
  var TOP = 10, YM = 0.26, SC = 215 / YM;
  function px(x) { return L + (x - XA) / (XB - XA) * (R - L); }
  function py(y) { return TOP + (YM - y) * SC; }
  function pdf(x, m) { return Math.exp(-0.5 * Math.pow((x - m) / SE, 2)) / (SE * Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI)); }
  function erf(x) { var s = x < 0 ? -1 : 1; x = Math.abs(x); var t = 1 / (1 + 0.3275911 * x);
    return s * (1 - (((((1.061405429 * t - 1.453152027) * t) + 1.421413741) * t - 0.284496736) * t + 0.254829592) * t * Math.exp(-x * x)); }
  function Phi(z) { return 0.5 * (1 + erf(z / Math.SQRT2)); }
  var svg = document.getElementById("du-svg"), sl = document.getElementById("du-mu"), lab = document.getElementById("du-mu-val"), out = document.getElementById("du-out");
  function path(m, lo, hi) {
    var d = "M" + px(lo).toFixed(1) + "," + py(0).toFixed(1);
    for (var x = lo; x <= hi + 1e-9; x += 0.01) d += " L" + px(x).toFixed(1) + "," + py(pdf(x, m)).toFixed(1);
    return d + " L" + px(hi).toFixed(1) + "," + py(0).toFixed(1) + " Z";
  }
  function draw() {
    var m = +sl.value, dist = Math.abs(XO - m), p = 2 * (1 - Phi(dist / SE)), g = "";
    lab.textContent = m.toFixed(2);
    var lo = m - 4 * SE, hi = m + 4 * SE;
    if (m - dist > lo) g += '<path d="' + path(m, lo, m - dist) + '" fill="#c53030" fill-opacity="0.4"/>';
    if (m + dist < hi) g += '<path d="' + path(m, m + dist, hi) + '" fill="#c53030" fill-opacity="0.4"/>';
    var d = "";
    for (var x = lo; x <= hi + 1e-9; x += 0.01) d += (d ? " L" : "M") + px(x).toFixed(1) + "," + py(pdf(x, m)).toFixed(1);
    g += '<path d="' + d + '" fill="none" stroke="#444" stroke-width="2.5"/>';
    g += '<line x1="' + L + '" y1="' + py(0) + '" x2="' + R + '" y2="' + py(0) + '" stroke="#52606d" stroke-width="2"/>';
    for (var t = 156; t <= 180; t += 4) g += '<text x="' + px(t) + '" y="' + (py(0) + 20) + '" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="#52606d">' + t + '</text>';
    g += '<line x1="' + px(XO) + '" y1="' + TOP + '" x2="' + px(XO) + '" y2="' + py(0) + '" stroke="#1f2933" stroke-width="3"/>' +
         '<text x="' + (px(XO) + (m < XO ? 8 : -8)) + '" y="' + (TOP + 14) + '" text-anchor="' + (m < XO ? "start" : "end") + '" font-size="17" font-weight="700" fill="#1f2933">X̄ = 170</text>';
    g += '<line x1="' + px(m) + '" y1="' + TOP + '" x2="' + px(m) + '" y2="' + py(0) + '" stroke="#2b6cb0" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-dasharray="6 5"/>' +
         '<text x="' + (px(m) + (m < XO ? -8 : 8)) + '" y="' + (TOP + 14) + '" text-anchor="' + (m < XO ? "end" : "start") + '" font-size="17" font-weight="700" fill="#2b6cb0">μ₀ = ' + m.toFixed(2) + '</text>';
    [[1.645, "#440154", "90% CI", 262], [1.96, "#21918c", "95% CI", 274], [2.576, "#fde725", "99% CI", 286]].forEach(function (c) {
      g += '<line x1="' + px(XO - c[0] * SE) + '" y1="' + c[3] + '" x2="' + px(XO + c[0] * SE) + '" y2="' + c[3] + '" stroke="' + c[1] + '" stroke-width="7"/>';
    });
    [["#440154", "90% CI", 24], ["#21918c", "95% CI", 46], ["#fde725", "99% CI", 68]].forEach(function (c) {
      g += '<circle cx="790" cy="' + c[2] + '" r="6" fill="' + c[0] + '"/><text x="805" y="' + (c[2] + 6) + '" font-size="17" fill="#1f2933">' + c[1] + '</text>';
    });
    svg.innerHTML = g;
    out.innerHTML = 'Shaded area (p-value): <b style="color:#c53030">' + p.toFixed(4) + '</b> &nbsp;·&nbsp; ' +
      [[0.10, "90%"], [0.05, "95%"], [0.01, "99%"]].map(function (c) {
        return 'α = ' + c[0].toFixed(2) + ': ' + (p < c[0] ? '<b>reject</b>' : 'fail to reject') + ' (μ₀ ' + (p < c[0] ? 'outside' : 'inside') + ' the ' + c[1] + ' CI)';
      }).join(' &nbsp;·&nbsp; ');
  }
  sl.addEventListener("input", draw); draw();
})();
</script>

## The duality

::: {.box .key}
At level $\alpha$, a two-sided test **rejects** $\mu_0$ exactly when $\mu_0$ lies **outside** the $(1-\alpha)$ confidence interval.
:::

. . .

::: {.box}
The confidence interval is the set of **all** values $\mu_0$ that the test would **not** reject: the plausible values.
:::

. . .

::: {.box .good}
<span class="tag">Our data</span>
$167$ is inside the 95% interval $[166.49,\ 173.51]$ (fail to reject at 5%) but outside the 90% interval $[167.06,\ 172.94]$ (reject at 10%). These are the intervals from the estimation lecture.
:::

## The two-sided test: summary

| Step | Two-sided test of $\mu$ ($\sigma$ known) | Our data |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **1. Hypotheses** | $H_0:\ \mu=\mu_0$<br>$H_1:\ \mu\mathrel{\rlap{\,/}{=}}\mu_0$ | $H_0:\ \mu=167$<br>$H_1:\ \mu\mathrel{\rlap{\,/}{=}}167$ |
| **2. Statistic** | $z=\dfrac{\bar{X}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}$ | $z\approx1.68$ |
| **3. P-value** | $2\,P(Z>\lvert z\rvert)$ | $p\approx0.093$ |
| **4. Decision** | reject if $p<\alpha$, equivalently $\lvert z\rvert>z_{\alpha/2}$ | $\alpha=0.05$: fail to reject |


# One-sided tests {.section-slide}

When the question has a direction.

## A one-sided question

::: {.cards}
::: {.box .c}
<span class="tag">Before: two-sided</span>
Is the average height of students **equal** to $167$ cm?

Any difference counts: taller **or** shorter.
:::
::: {.box .key .c}
<span class="tag">Now: one-sided</span>
Are students **taller** than $167$ cm?

Only one direction counts.
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.box .good}
The direction comes from the **claim we want to check**, not from the data.
:::

## Which samples make us doubt?

::: {.box}
<span class="tag">The claim and its opposite</span>
Claim to check: students are **taller** than $167$ cm. The opposite, our benchmark $H_0$: students are **not taller** (the mean is $167$ or less).
:::

. . .

::: {.box .key}
Three possible sample means. Does each one make you **doubt** $H_0$?
:::

## Which samples make us doubt? The answers

::: {.cards}
::: {.box .warn .c}
<span class="tag">$\bar{X}=180$</span>
**Yes**, strongly. Far above $167$.
:::
::: {.box .c}
<span class="tag">$\bar{X}=167$</span>
**No.** Exactly what $H_0$ expects.
:::
::: {.box .good .c}
<span class="tag">$\bar{X}=150$</span>
**No.** Far from $167$, but on the wrong side: if anything it **supports** $H_0$.
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.box}
<span class="tag">Compare</span>
With the two-sided question ("equal to $167$?"), $\bar{X}=150$ **would** have made us doubt.
:::

## Evidence against $H_0$

::: {.box .key}
<span class="tag">Big idea</span>
**Evidence against $H_0$ is evidence pointing toward $H_1$.**
:::

. . .

::: {.box}
A sample is surprising under $H_0$ only if it is unusual **in the direction the claim points**. A sample on the other side is not surprising: it is exactly what $H_0$ expects, because "not taller" includes **all** lower means.
:::

. . .

::: {.box .good}
So "far from $167$" is no longer the criterion. The criterion is "far from $167$ **in the direction of $H_1$**".
:::

## Easier or harder to reject?

::: {.box .key}
<span class="tag">Question</span>
Compared with the two-sided question, is it **easier or harder** to reject $H_0$ in a one-sided test?
:::

. . .

::: {.box}
Think about what counts as "a sample at least as surprising as ours". Two-sided: far from $167$ in **either** direction. One-sided: far **above** $167$ only.
:::

## Easier or harder? The answer

::: {.cards}
::: {.box .good .c}
<span class="tag">In the direction of $H_1$: easier</span>
Only one tail is counted, so the same sample looks **more surprising**: its p-value is **half** the two-sided one.
:::
::: {.box .warn .c}
<span class="tag">In the other direction: impossible</span>
A sample like $\bar{X}=150$ can **never** make us reject, however far it is from $167$.
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.box .key}
A one-sided test is a **bet on a direction**: stronger if right, blind if wrong. So choose the direction **before** seeing the data.
:::

## One-sided example: the data

::: {.box}
<span class="tag">Question</span>
Are students **taller** than $167$ cm? Data: $n=20$, $\bar{X}=170$, $\sigma=8$ (known), so $SE=8/\sqrt{20}\approx1.789$.
:::

. . .

::: {.box .key}
The **same data** as in the two-sided test. Only the question has changed, so the verdict may change too.
:::

## One-sided example: the hypotheses

::: {.box .key}
The claim goes into $H_1$. $H_0$ is its opposite: "not taller".
$$H_0:\ \mu\leq167 \qquad H_1:\ \mu>167$$
:::

. . .

::: {.box}
<span class="tag">$H_0$ can now be an inequality</span>
$H_0$ still contains an equality sign, but it now covers a whole range of values: every $\mu\leq167$.
:::

. . .

::: {.box .good}
<span class="tag">Reformulate with an equality</span>
Among all $\mu\leq167$, the hardest value to reject is $167$ itself: a sample mean of $170$ would be **even more surprising** if the true mean were lower, say $160$. So if we can reject $\mu=167$, we reject every lower value too, and it is enough to test
$$H_0:\ \mu=167 \qquad H_1:\ \mu>167$$
:::

## One-sided example: the test

::: {.box}
$$z=\frac{170-167}{1.789}\approx1.68$$
The same statistic as in the two-sided test: it does not depend on the direction.
:::

. . .

::: {.cards}
::: {.box .c}
<span class="tag">P-value</span>
Only the **upper** tail counts: $p=P(Z>1.68)\approx0.047$.
:::
::: {.box .c}
<span class="tag">Critical value</span>
At $\alpha=0.05$ the whole $\alpha$ sits in the upper tail: reject if $z>1.645$.
:::
:::

## One-sided example: decision

::: {.box .key}
$H_0:\ \mu=167$ against $H_1:\ \mu>167$, $\alpha=0.05$.<br>
$p\approx0.047<0.05$, and $z=1.68>1.645$: **reject $H_0$**.
:::

. . .

::: {.box .good}
<span class="tag">Conclusion</span>
At the 5% level there **is sufficient evidence** that the average height of students is **greater than $167$ cm**.
:::

. . .

::: {.box .warn}
<span class="tag">Compare</span>
The same data did **not** reject in the two-sided test ($p=0.093$): the one-sided p-value is **half** as large. This is legitimate only if the direction was chosen **before** seeing the data.
:::

## One-sided test: the picture

::: {.cap}
Shaded: the probability of a result as high as $\bar{X}=170$ if the slider value were the true $\mu_0$, for $H_1:\mu>\mu_0$.
:::

(function () {
  var SE = 8 / Math.sqrt(20), XO = 170, L = 50, R = 880, XA = 155, XB = 181;
  var TOP = 10, YM = 0.26, SC = 215 / YM;
  function px(x) { return L + (x - XA) / (XB - XA) * (R - L); }
  function py(y) { return TOP + (YM - y) * SC; }
  function pdf(x, m) { return Math.exp(-0.5 * Math.pow((x - m) / SE, 2)) / (SE * Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI)); }
  function erf(x) { var s = x < 0 ? -1 : 1; x = Math.abs(x); var t = 1 / (1 + 0.3275911 * x);
    return s * (1 - (((((1.061405429 * t - 1.453152027) * t) + 1.421413741) * t - 0.284496736) * t + 0.254829592) * t * Math.exp(-x * x)); }
  function Phi(z) { return 0.5 * (1 + erf(z / Math.SQRT2)); }
  var svg = document.getElementById("os-svg"), sl = document.getElementById("os-mu"), lab = document.getElementById("os-mu-val"), out = document.getElementById("os-out");
  function draw() {
    var m = +sl.value, p = 1 - Phi((XO - m) / SE), g = "";
    lab.textContent = m.toFixed(2);
    var lo = m - 4 * SE, hi = m + 4 * SE;
    if (XO < hi) {
      var d0 = "M" + px(Math.max(XO, lo)).toFixed(1) + "," + py(0).toFixed(1);
      for (var x = Math.max(XO, lo); x <= hi + 1e-9; x += 0.01) d0 += " L" + px(x).toFixed(1) + "," + py(pdf(x, m)).toFixed(1);
      g += '<path d="' + d0 + ' L' + px(hi).toFixed(1) + ',' + py(0).toFixed(1) + ' Z" fill="#c53030" fill-opacity="0.4"/>';
    }
    var d = "";
    for (var x2 = lo; x2 <= hi + 1e-9; x2 += 0.01) d += (d ? " L" : "M") + px(x2).toFixed(1) + "," + py(pdf(x2, m)).toFixed(1);
    g += '<path d="' + d + '" fill="none" stroke="#444" stroke-width="2.5"/>';
    g += '<line x1="' + L + '" y1="' + py(0) + '" x2="' + R + '" y2="' + py(0) + '" stroke="#52606d" stroke-width="2"/>';
    for (var t = 156; t <= 180; t += 4) g += '<text x="' + px(t) + '" y="' + (py(0) + 20) + '" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="#52606d">' + t + '</text>';
    g += '<line x1="' + px(XO) + '" y1="' + TOP + '" x2="' + px(XO) + '" y2="' + py(0) + '" stroke="#1f2933" stroke-width="3"/>' +
         '<text x="' + (px(XO) + (m < XO ? 8 : -8)) + '" y="' + (TOP + 14) + '" text-anchor="' + (m < XO ? "start" : "end") + '" font-size="17" font-weight="700" fill="#1f2933">X̄ = 170</text>';
    g += '<line x1="' + px(m) + '" y1="' + TOP + '" x2="' + px(m) + '" y2="' + py(0) + '" stroke="#2b6cb0" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-dasharray="6 5"/>' +
         '<text x="' + (px(m) + (m < XO ? -8 : 8)) + '" y="' + (TOP + 14) + '" text-anchor="' + (m < XO ? "end" : "start") + '" font-size="17" font-weight="700" fill="#2b6cb0">μ₀ = ' + m.toFixed(2) + '</text>';
    // one-sided bounds (H1: mu > mu0): mu0 is rejected at level a when it lies below XO - z_a * SE
    [[1.282, "#440154", 262], [1.645, "#21918c", 274], [2.326, "#fde725", 286]].forEach(function (c) {
      g += '<line x1="' + px(XO - c[0] * SE) + '" y1="' + c[2] + '" x2="' + R + '" y2="' + c[2] + '" stroke="' + c[1] + '" stroke-width="7"/>';
    });
    [["#440154", "α = 0.10", 24], ["#21918c", "α = 0.05", 46], ["#fde725", "α = 0.01", 68]].forEach(function (c) {
      g += '<circle cx="790" cy="' + c[2] + '" r="6" fill="' + c[0] + '"/><text x="805" y="' + (c[2] + 6) + '" font-size="17" fill="#1f2933">' + c[1] + '</text>';
    });
    svg.innerHTML = g;
    out.innerHTML = 'One-sided p-value (shaded area): <b style="color:#c53030">' + p.toFixed(4) + '</b> &nbsp;·&nbsp; ' +
      [0.10, 0.05, 0.01].map(function (a) { return 'α = ' + a.toFixed(2) + ': ' + (p < a ? '<b>reject</b>' : 'fail to reject'); }).join(' &nbsp;·&nbsp; ') +
      '<br>Each bar: the values of μ₀ that are <b>not</b> rejected at that α.';
  }
  sl.addEventListener("input", draw); draw();
})();
</script>

## Two-sided vs. one-sided

| | Two-sided | One-sided |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Question** | Is there *any* difference? | Is there an *increase* or a *decrease*? |
| **Alternative $H_1$** | $\mu\mathrel{\rlap{\,/}{=}}\mu_0$ | $\mu>\mu_0$ or $\mu<\mu_0$ |
| **Rejection region** | Two tails, $\alpha/2$ each | One tail, the full $\alpha$ |
| **P-value** | $2\,P(Z>\lvert z\rvert)$ | Area in the tail named by $H_1$ |

## Tail areas and power

::: {.box}
<span class="tag">Tail areas</span>
In a **two-sided** test $\alpha$ is split between the lower and upper tails. In a **one-sided** test the whole $\alpha$ goes into the tail named by $H_1$.
:::

. . .

::: {.box .key}
<span class="tag">Key result: power</span>
A one-sided test is more **powerful** in the hypothesized direction: its critical value is closer to the mean. But it completely ignores effects in the opposite direction.
:::

# Testing $\mu$ when $\sigma$ is unknown {.section-slide}

Replace $\sigma$ by its estimate $s$.

## The t-statistic

::: {.box}
So far $\sigma$ was **known**. In practice it is unknown and must be estimated by the sample standard deviation $s$.
:::

. . .

::: {.box .key}
<span class="tag">Definition</span>
$$t=\frac{\bar{X}-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt n}$$
where $s$ is the sample standard deviation.
:::

## Its distribution

::: {.box .key}
<span class="tag">Key result</span>
Draw a random sample of size $n$ from a **normal population** with mean $\mu$. Then
$$t=\frac{\bar{X}-\mu}{s/\sqrt n}$$
follows the **Student's $t$-distribution** with $n-1$ degrees of freedom. Under $H_0$, $\mu=\mu_0$.
:::

. . .

::: {.box}
<span class="tag">Degrees of freedom $df=n-1$</span>
The number of independent pieces of information used to estimate the standard deviation. The smaller the $df$, the **flatter** the curve and the **thicker** the tails.
:::

## The t-distribution vs. the normal

::: {.cap}
Solid red: Student's $t$. Dashed black: the standard normal. Move the slider to change $df$.
:::

<svg id="td-svg" viewBox="0 0 900 300" class="famplot"></svg>

<div class="ctl" style="justify-content:center">
  <label>Degrees of freedom: <input type="range" id="td-df" min="1" max="50" step="1" value="3" style="width:420px"> <b id="td-df-val">3</b></label>
</div>

<script>
(function () {
  var L = 50, R = 880, XA = -3.5, XB = 3.5, TOP = 20, B = 250, YM = 0.45;
  function px(x) { return L + (x - XA) / (XB - XA) * (R - L); }
  function py(y) { return B - y / YM * (B - TOP); }
  function lgamma(z) {
    var C = [76.18009172947146, -86.50532032941677, 24.01409824083091, -1.231739572450155, 0.1208650973866179e-2, -0.5395239384953e-5];
    var y = z, tmp = z + 5.5; tmp -= (z + 0.5) * Math.log(tmp);
    var ser = 1.000000000190015;
    for (var j = 0; j < 6; j++) ser += C[j] / ++y;
    return -tmp + Math.log(2.5066282746310005 * ser / z);
  }
  function tpdf(x, v) { return Math.exp(lgamma((v + 1) / 2) - lgamma(v / 2)) / Math.sqrt(v * Math.PI) * Math.pow(1 + x * x / v, -(v + 1) / 2); }
  function npdf(x) { return Math.exp(-0.5 * x * x) / Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI); }
  var svg = document.getElementById("td-svg"), sl = document.getElementById("td-df"), lab = document.getElementById("td-df-val");
  function draw() {
    var v = +sl.value, g = "", dn = "", dt = "";
    lab.textContent = v;
    for (var x = XA; x <= XB + 1e-9; x += 0.02) {
      dn += (dn ? " L" : "M") + px(x).toFixed(1) + "," + py(npdf(x)).toFixed(1);
      dt += (dt ? " L" : "M") + px(x).toFixed(1) + "," + py(tpdf(x, v)).toFixed(1);
    }
    g += '<line x1="' + L + '" y1="' + B + '" x2="' + R + '" y2="' + B + '" stroke="#52606d" stroke-width="2"/>';
    for (var t = -3; t <= 3; t++) g += '<text x="' + px(t) + '" y="' + (B + 22) + '" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="#52606d">' + t + '</text>';
    g += '<text x="' + ((L + R) / 2) + '" y="' + (B + 46) + '" text-anchor="middle" font-size="17" fill="#1f2933">t-statistic / z-score</text>';
    g += '<path d="' + dn + '" fill="none" stroke="#1f2933" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-dasharray="7 5"/>';
    g += '<path d="' + dt + '" fill="none" stroke="#c53030" stroke-width="3"/>';
    g += '<line x1="660" y1="40" x2="700" y2="40" stroke="#1f2933" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-dasharray="7 5"/><text x="710" y="46" font-size="17" fill="#1f2933">Standard normal</text>';
    g += '<line x1="660" y1="68" x2="700" y2="68" stroke="#c53030" stroke-width="3"/><text x="710" y="74" font-size="17" font-weight="700" fill="#c53030">Student\'s t (df = ' + v + ')</text>';
    svg.innerHTML = g;
  }
  sl.addEventListener("input", draw); draw();
})();
</script>

## Normal vs. t

| Feature | Standard normal ($z$) | Student's $t$ |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Shape** | Bell-shaped, symmetric | Bell-shaped, symmetric |
| **Tails** | Thin | **Thicker (heavier)** |
| **Spread** | Constant | Depends on $df=n-1$ |
| **Convergence** | The "ideal" | Approaches the normal as $n\to\infty$ |

## The cost of uncertainty

::: {.box .key}
Because the $t$-distribution has thicker tails, its **critical values** are always larger than those of the $z$-test at the same $\alpha$.
:::

. . .

::: {.cards}
::: {.box .warn}
P-values are **larger** for the same statistic: harder to reject $H_0$.
:::
::: {.box .warn}
Confidence intervals are **wider**: more uncertainty.
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.box .good}
As $n$ grows, the $t$-distribution converges to the standard normal, so critical values and p-values become close to those of the $z$-test.
:::

. . .

::: {.cap}
Self-study: learn how to use the $t$-table at the end of the book.
:::

## A worked t-test

::: {.box .key}
<span class="tag">Same question, $\sigma$ unknown</span>
Is the average height of students equal to $167$ cm? Data: $n=20$, $\bar{X}=170$, and now $\sigma$ is unknown: suppose the sample SD is $s=8$.
$$H_0:\ \mu=167 \qquad H_1:\ \mu\mathrel{\rlap{\,/}{=}}167$$
:::

. . .

::: {.box}
$$t=\frac{170-167}{8/\sqrt{20}}\approx1.68,\qquad df=n-1=19$$
:::

## A worked t-test: the decision

::: {.box}
$$t=\frac{170-167}{8/\sqrt{20}}\approx1.68,\qquad df=19$$
:::

. . .

::: {.cards}
::: {.box .c}
<span class="tag">Critical value</span>
$t_{0.025,\,19}\approx2.093$, larger than $z_{0.025}=1.96$. $|t|=1.68<2.093$.
:::
::: {.box .c}
<span class="tag">P-value</span>
$p=2\,P(T_{19}>1.68)\approx0.110$, **larger** than the $z$-test's $0.093$.
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.box .good}
<span class="tag">Conclusion</span>
At $\alpha=0.05$ we **fail to reject** $H_0$: there is not sufficient evidence that the mean height of students differs from $167$ cm. Note that at $\alpha=0.10$ the $z$-test rejected but the $t$-test does **not** ($0.110>0.10$): the cost of not knowing $\sigma$.
:::

## The whole procedure on one page

| Step | What we do |
|:--|:--|
| **1. Hypotheses** | $H_0$ with $=$ (the benchmark $\mu_0$); $H_1$ is $\mathrel{\rlap{\,/}{=}}$, $>$ or $<$. |
| **2. Statistic** | $\sigma$ known: $z=\dfrac{\bar{X}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}$. $\sigma$ unknown: $t=\dfrac{\bar{X}-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt n}$ with $df=n-1$. |
| **3. P-value** | $\mathrel{\rlap{\,/}{=}}$: both tails, $2\,P(\text{beyond }\lvert\text{stat}\rvert)$. $>$: upper tail. $<$: lower tail. |
| **4. Decision** | $p<\alpha$ (or statistic beyond the critical value): **reject $H_0$**. Otherwise: **fail to reject**. |

. . .

::: {.box .key}
<span class="tag">Always finish with a sentence</span>
"At the $\alpha$ level there **is / is not sufficient evidence** that $\ldots$ (the claim in $H_1$)."
:::
